item.accessInformation: Conservation International
item.description:
First defined in 1988 by scientist Norman Myers, biodiversity hotspots are areas characterized by high levels of endemic plants coupled with significant habitat loss. Specifically, a region must meet the following criteria to achieve Conservation International’s hotspot classification:At least 1,500 species of vascular plants (>0.5% of the world’s total) are endemicAt least 70% of the original natural vegetation has been lost

When Myers first defined the term, he identified 10 tropical forest hotspots. The need to pinpoint priority conservation regions led Conservation International (CI) to adopt the term and reassess the hotspot concept. In this process, CI introduced quantitative thresholds (see above) and added additional regions. At that time, there were 25 hotspots. Because of the constant change in environmental threats and the improved understanding of biodiversity, CI has since revisited the hotspots to refine boundaries, update information, and add new regions. This process produced an additional 10 hotspots, bringing the total to 35.
item.licenseInfo: This layer only displays the land-based portion of biodiversity hotspots, although some hotspots extend offshore
item.snippet: Displays Conservation International’s biodiversity hotspots—defined regions around the world where biodiversity conservation is most urgent because of high levels of endemism and human threat
item.title: Biodiversity Hotspots

item.description:
Valori più recenti degli indicatori statistici del Report Last20 2026 per i 20 paesi del gruppo L20: Afghanistan, Burkina Faso, Burundi, Ciad, Eritrea, Haiti, Libano, Liberia, Madagascar, Malawi, Mali, Mozambico, Niger, Repubblica Centrafricana, Repubblica Democratica del Congo, Siria, Somalia, Sud Sudan, Sudan e Yemen. 

Per ciascuna delle 39 tavole del report è riportato solo l'ultimo valore disponibile, senza serie storiche né variazioni. I campi coprono otto dimensioni: economico-finanziaria, demografica, sociale e dei diritti fondamentali, istituzionale e governance, conflitti e sicurezza, climatica e ambientale, mobilità umana e sistema-mondo. 

Ogni record corrisponde a un paese ed è identificato dal codice ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 (ISO_Code), chiave di join con i poligoni dei paesi. Quando l'indicatore è riportato come "più recente", un campo dedicato indica l'anno di riferimento, che può variare da paese a paese; negli altri casi l'anno è nel nome del campo (es. 2025). 

I dati non disponibili sono lasciati vuoti. Per il Global Hunger Index 2025 i valori di Burundi, Sudan e Yemen sono il punto medio dell'intervallo provvisorio pubblicato e sono accompagnati da una nota. 

Le fonti sono indicate per ciascun campo e comprendono, tra le altre, Banca Mondiale, FMI, UN DESA, Fund for Peace, Global Hunger Index e UCDP.

item.description: The biodiversity hotspots are regions known to hold especially high numbers of species found nowhere else, yet their remaining habitat combined covers a little more than two percent of Earth's land surface. According to the criteria developed by Myers et al. (2000), a hotspot must meet two thresholds in order to qualify: 1) it must have at least 1500 endemic, native vascular plant species, and 2) it must have already lost at least 70% of its primary, native vegetation. In the updated analysis, Mittermeier et al. (2004) recognize 34 hotspots which together hold 50% of the world's plant species and 42% of all terrestrial vertebrates as endemics. As evidence of their urgency for global conservation, hotspots also hold exceptionally high numbers of threatened vertebrates, including 50% of threatened mammals, 73% of threatened birds and 79% of threatened amphibians as endemics. There are an estimated two billion people living in the hotspots, with 300 million people within less than 10 km of existing protected areas.
item.snippet: To show the location and extent of the 35 biodiversity hotspots (highly threatened biogeographic regions with high-biodiversity endemism), as defined by Mittermeier et al. (2011).
item.title: Biodiversity Hotspots (2016)

item.description:
The SSSI IRZs are a Geographical Information System (GIS) tool developed by Natural England to make rapid initial assessment of the potential risks posed by development proposals to SSSIs and those Special Areas of Conservation (SACs), Special Protection Areas (SPAs) or Ramsar sites that they underpin. They define zones around each site which reflect the sensitivities of the features for which the site is notified and indicate the types of development proposal which could potentially have adverse impacts and need further consideration. In certain locations they also include Natural England’s statutory advice for certain development types.

LPAs can use the SSSI IRZs to consider if a proposed development is likely to affect a terrestrial SSSI and those SACs, SPAs or Ramsar sites that they underpin and when to consult Natural England to seek advice.  Where the SSSI IRZs include Natural England’s statutory advice or indicate a risk is unlikely, LPAs can use the SSSI IRZs to instantly generate a formal consultation response.

Add the SSSI IRZs to your own GIS using the Web Map Service (WMS) link or download from the dropdown menu above or the links below.

  • Download the latest update in ESRI Shapefile format.

Use the SSSI IRZs online on the MAGIC website.

View the SSSI IRZs user guidance to learn how to interpret and use the SSSI IRZs.

For information on when LPAs must consult Natural England when considering development proposals refer to Planning and transport authorities: get environmental advice on planning - GOV.UK (www.gov.uk).

For information on how developers can get advice from Natural England on planning applications refer to Developers: get environmental advice on your planning proposals - GOV.UK (www.gov.uk).

Full metadata can be viewed on data.gov.uk.
item.snippet: The Impact Risk Zones for Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI IRZs) are for local planning authorities (LPAs) to determine if a proposed development is likely to affect a terrestrial SSSI and when to consult Natural England.

item.description:
OS Open Rivers is a generalised open water network showing the flow and the locations of rivers, streams, lakes and canals across the whole of Great Britain. The new product is part of the OS Open suite and is designed to be used with other OpenData product sets. It’s mapping that can help you question, visualise and share results quickly and clearly. 
 

 

With OS Open Rivers you can: 

  • Understand the water network at a ‘high level’ with generalised geometry and network connectivity.
     
  • View a network of main rivers, identifying the main river course along its full length.
     
  • Pin information on the connected network for personal or business use. 
     
  • Take an informed overview of a situation along the network to manage it strategically. 
     
  • Compare and monitor stretches of water. 
     
  • Share information, such as flood alerts and flood risk areas.

For more information on OS Rivers see their product page: https://www.ordnancesurvey.co.uk/products/os-open-rivers

 

The currency of this data is 04/2026 The coverage of the map service is GB.

item.description:
Il dataset raccoglie tutti gli indicatori statistici del Report Last20 2026 per i 20 paesi del gruppo L20: Afghanistan, Burkina Faso, Burundi, Ciad, Eritrea, Haiti, Libano, Liberia, Madagascar, Malawi, Mali, Mozambico, Niger, Repubblica Centrafricana, Repubblica Democratica del Congo, Siria, Somalia, Sud Sudan, Sudan e Yemen. 

I 213 campi provengono dalle 39 tavole del report, organizzate in otto dimensioni: economico-finanziaria, demografica, sociale e dei diritti fondamentali, istituzionale e governance, conflitti e sicurezza, climatica e ambientale, mobilità umana e sistema-mondo. 

Per ogni indicatore sono riportati i valori per gli anni di riferimento della tavola (ad esempio 2005, 2015, 2020, 2025), il valore più recente e la variazione nel periodo. 

Ogni record corrisponde a un paese ed è identificato dal codice ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 (ISO_Code), chiave di join con i poligoni dei paesi. 

Ci sono alcune convenzioni da tenere presenti: Anno di riferimento: dove il dato è "più recente" o riferito a un anno diverso da quello della colonna, un campo dedicato indica l'anno, che può variare da paese a paese.

Variazioni percentuali: sono espresse in punti percentuali, quindi 87.1 corrisponde a +87,1%. Le altre variazioni sono nell'unità dell'indicatore. 

Global Hunger Index 2025: per Burundi, Sudan e Yemen il valore è il punto medio dell'intervallo provvisorio pubblicato, accompagnato da una nota. 

Dati mancanti: i dati non disponibili sono lasciati vuoti. Valori di sintesi: medie e mediane L20, media G20 e totali del report non sono inclusi nei record. 

Le fonti sono indicate per ciascun campo e comprendono, tra le altre, Banca Mondiale, FMI, UN DESA, Fund for Peace, Global Hunger Index e UCDP.

item.description:
Apparent Visible Wavelength (AVW) from the NASA Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) Ocean Color Instrument (OCI). The AVW data product leverages OCI's continuous, hyperspectral set of remote sensing reflectance wavelengths spanning the visible spectrum (from 400-700 nanometers, nm) to calculate AVW in units of nm, a single value describing the dominant color of the water being observed (Vandermeulen et al. 2020; Vandermeulen and Cetinic 2024). AVW is provided as global, 8-day averages mapped to a standard, equal-angle, latitude-longitude grid of approximately 0.04 degrees, or 4 kilometers (km) at the equator. Pixels with no data values are masked (excluded) due to presence of land, cloud cover, or other features marked by quality control flags as described below.


Data Layer Summary
Name, units Apparent Visible Wavelength
[nm]		 Apparent visible wavelength, a measure of ocean color, in units of nanometers (nm)
Spatial resolution 4 km2 Level-3, mapped to standard grid, global coverage
Time Resolution 8 day average Each pixel represents an average of the valid, daily values observed within that grid element during the 8-day interval (approx 1 week).

Note: 8 day average data layer is calculated from daily, "refined" (archive-quality) Level 3 PACE AVW products, which are available at NASA Earthdata via this link in NetCDF format as part of the Apparent Optical Properties (AOP) suite. NASA Earthdata account required to download.

Data Version Version 3.2 Data versions change as improved calibration, validation, algorithm refinements, etc are applied over time. See Version 3.2 Release Notes for details.
Latency ̃1 month This imagery service provides “refined” (archive-quality) PACE data products from March 2024-present, which have an approx 1 month latency.

Note: Lower latency “near real time (NRT)” Level 3 PACE AVW products are available at NASA Earthdata via this link in NetCDF format as part of the Apparent Optical Properties (AOP) suite. Latency typically <24 hours. NASA Earthdata account required to download.

What can I do with this layer?
AVW is simple and intuitive spectral classification tool that enables a more manageable handling of complex spectral information for aquatic science applications (Vandermeulen et al. 2020). Changing values in AVW are a measure of change in the ocean's dominant color: lower AVW values represent more clear water and higher values represent more turbid water. AVW is a useful as an optical water-type index, partitioning a region's ocean observations into types relevant to water quality and marine ecosystem processes. Additionally, AVW can be applied to datasets of varying multi- and hyperspectral resolutions. This provides continuity between PACE AVW and AVW from heritage satellite ocean color sensors (those launched prior to PACE), enabling examination of longer term (up to decadal) trends of AVW in a given region (Vandermeulen et al. 2020; Vandermeulen and Cetinic 2024). The time (8 day average) and space (4 km2) resolution of this data layer supports weekly to seasonal and annual insight at sub-regional to global scales.


What should I know about the data?
Data Status (Maturity): This product is provisional, which means that product results have been reviewed and are in family with heritage data products or other basis of expectation, but have not yet been extensively validated and so may still contain significant errors. Data layer is sufficient for qualitative determinations of product fitness-for-purpose, for testing by operational users, and may be suitable for scientific publication.


Data Masking: These products are Level 3, globally-binned products from NASA’s Ocean Biology Processing Group (OBPG), which by default are masked (pixel data value is set to null, or no data) according to a standard set of quality control parameters. For a list of these parameters, see the third column of the table included here: https://oceancolor.gsfc.nasa.gov/resources/atbd/ocl2flags/.


Algorithm Theoretical Basis Document (ATBD): See ATBD for algorithm details including scientific theory, calculations, etc. at DOI 10.5067/KAROCHG01RYJ.


Where do I go with further questions?
Visit NASA’s Earthdata Forum where users can post questions that are answered by the personnel working at NASA with the PACE mission and/or the Ocean Biology Distributed Active Archive Center (OB.DAAC) that processes and distributes PACE data. First, follow this link to view only “PACE” and “OBDAAC” tagged questions on the Earthdata Forum. Then search and read through previous posts for your question. If it has not yet been asked please post your question in the Forum and be sure "PACE" and "OBDAAC" filter tags are applied.



Mission and Product Background

PACE Mission Overview:
Launched in February 2024, NASA’s Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) observatory uniquely provides near-daily, hyperspectral coverage of Earth’s surface, plus hyperspectral and hyperangular polarimetry. PACE is a comprehensive Earth System mission, delivering all new, space-based information on the health and diversity of aquatic and terrestrial life (algae, plants), aerosol properties & modes (e.g. smoke, dust), cloud types, and more.


The Ocean Color Instrument (OCI), PACE's primary sensor, is a hyperspectral (5 nm resolution) imaging spectrometer that measures properties of light from the ultraviolet (UV, 340 nm) through visible and near infrared (NIR, 895 nm) portions of the electromagnetic spectrum in 1.25 to 2.5 nm steps, plus 7 shortwave infrared (SWIR) bands (Werdell et al. 2019). Observations from OCI are moderate spatial resolution (1.2 km2), enabling a relatively frequent revisit time of 1-2 days. This combination of continuous, global coverage and spectral capabilities is unmatched by any other satellite platform, public or private. PACE benefits society by expanding our foundational knowledge of Earth and enabling novel, space-based science and applications tools across water resources (e.g. fisheries), air quality, land monitoring & management, and more.


What does AVW represent and how is it calculated?
AVW is a one-dimensional geophysical metric that is inherently correlated to ocean color, as defined by the remote sensing reflectance (R(λ)rs) spectral shape across the visible region of the spectrum (400-700 nm; Vandermeulen et al. 2020). R(λ)rs, the AVW algorithm input, is used to calculate the weighted harmonic mean of the wavelengths. Output is an AVW in units of nm, a quantitative descriptor of weighted mean color reflected from the water's surface. PACE AVW spans PACE's continuous hyperspectral R(λ)rs observations across the visible spectrum while AVW from heritage multi-spectral sensors is calculated from their 4-10 available R(λ)rs channels (Vandermeulen and Cetinic 2024).


The entire visible spectrum is utilized in the calculation of AVW, affording the opportunity to describe and analyze spectral trends in R(λ)rs in terms of a single variable (Vandermeulen et al. 2020). This simplification allows for streamlined visualisation and monitoring of small changes in apparent color from highly complex optical data. AVW's dimensionality reduction of spectral information is a robust and user-friendly means to describe and analyze R(λ)rs in terms of spatial and temporal trends and variability. Also, AVW can be utilized across heritage and current ocean color sensors, allowing for continuity and long term monitoring of AVW in aquatic ecosystems.


What other PACE data layers are available?
This data layer is 1 of 11 PACE products initially selected for the Living Atlas catalog from the mission’s comprehensive aquatic, atmospheric, and terrestrial product catalog. Click here to view all 11 PACE Living Atlas imagery services. Global, hyperspectral remote sensing reflectance observations from OCI with over 250 spectral bands, and used to derive many of PACE's aquatic products, are available to download in NetCDF format from NASA Earthdata as Level 3, mapped data with 4 km2 resolution or as Level 2 granules at unprojected, native spatial resolution (no finer than 1.2km2). To learn more about obtaining PACE data from NASA, first learn about PACE data access here, next decide which product(s) you would like to use, then go to NASA Earthdata to find your product(s) of interest in NetCDF format, which can be downloaded and then imported into ArcGIS. To learn about using Earthdata Search to narrow your data product selection, watch this tutorial. An Earthdata account is needed to download data from NASA, sign up here.



How can I stay up to date with the PACE mission?

Join the PACE Community for mission news, events, new product release announcements, and to receive our newsletters.

Would you like to see imagery services for more PACE products? Please let us know here.

item.accessInformation: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Ocean Ecology Laboratory, Ocean Biology Processing Group. PACE OCI Level-3 Mapped Particulate backscattering Coefficient at 442 nm (bbp (442), GIOP model), Version 3.2 Data; NASA OB.DAAC, Greenbelt, MD, USA.
item.description:
Particulate backscattering coefficient at 442 nanometers (bbp (442)) from the NASA Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) Ocean Color Instrument (OCI). This bbp (442) data layer provides a proxy of water clarity overall as well as an estimate of suspended particulate constituents present in the water. bbp (442) is provided as global, 8-day averages mapped to a standard, equal-angle, latitude-longitude grid of approximately 0.04 degrees, or 4 kilometers (km) at the equator. Pixels with no data values are masked (excluded) due to presence of land, cloud cover, or other features marked by quality control flags as described below.


Data Layer Summary
Name, units Particulate Backscattering at 442 nm
[m-1]		 Backscattering coefficient of suspended particulate material at 442 nm in units of inverse meters (m-1)
Spatial resolution 4 km2 Level-3, mapped to standard grid, global coverage
Time Resolution 8 day average Each pixel represents an average of the valid, daily values observed within that grid element during the 8-day interval (approx 1 week).

Note: 8 day average data layer is calculated from daily, "refined" (archive-quality) Level 3 PACE bbp (442) products, which are available at NASA Earthdata via this link in NetCDF format as part of the Inherent Optical Properties (IOP) suite. NASA Earthdata account required to download.

Data Version Version 3.2 Data versions change as improved calibration, validation, algorithm refinements, etc are applied over time. See Version 3.2 Release Notes for details.
Latency ̃1 month This imagery service provides “refined” (archive-quality) PACE data products from March 2024-present, which have an approx 1 month latency.

Note: Lower latency “near real time (NRT)” Level 3 PACE bbp (442) data are available at NASA Earthdata via this link in NetCDF format as part of the Inherent Optical Properties (IOP) NRT suite. Latency typically <24 hours. NASA Earthdata account required to download.

What can I do with this layer?
The bbp (442) data layer supports water-type classification, water-clarity assessment, biogeochemical studies, and forward/adjoint radiative-transfer applications. As an inherent optical property (IOP, described in background information below), bbp (442) is more suitable for cross-sensor comparisons than apparent optical property (AOP) measurements, which vary with solar conditions at the time of measurement. The time (8 day average) and space (4 km2) resolution of this data layer enables weekly to seasonal and annual insight at sub-regional to global scales.


What should I know about the data?
Data Status (Maturity): This product is provisional, which means that product results have been reviewed and are in family with heritage data products or other basis of expectation, but have not yet been extensively validated and so may still contain significant errors. Data layer is sufficient for qualitative determinations of product fitness-for-purpose, for testing by operational users, and may be suitable for scientific publication.


Data Masking: These products are Level 3, globally-binned products from NASA’s Ocean Biology Processing Group (OBPG), which by default are masked (pixel data value is set to null, or no data) according to a standard set of quality control parameters. For a list of these parameters, see the third column of the table included here: https://oceancolor.gsfc.nasa.gov/resources/atbd/ocl2flags/.


Application of bbp (442) in varied water types: The Generalized Inherent Optical Properties framework in its default algorithm configuration (GIOP-DC; Werdell et al. 2013) used to derive bbp (442) was developed to maximize global performance. End users are advised to carefully consider the validity of retrievals in extreme conditions such as highly turbid, optically shallow, and inland/freshwater systems where values may carry higher uncertainty.


Algorithm Theoretical Basis Document (ATBD): See ATBD for algorithm details including scientific theory, calculations, etc. at DOI 10.5067/ZGBW3QECROJ2.


Where do I go with further questions?
Visit NASA’s Earthdata Forum where users can post questions that are answered by the personnel working at NASA with the PACE mission and/or the Ocean Biology Distributed Active Archive Center (OB.DAAC) that processes and distributes PACE data. First, follow this link to view only “PACE” and “OBDAAC” tagged questions on the Earthdata Forum. Then search and read through previous posts for your question. If it has not yet been asked please post your question in the Forum and be sure "PACE" and "OBDAAC" filter tags are applied.



Mission and Product Background

PACE Mission Overview:
Launched in February 2024, NASA’s Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) observatory uniquely provides near-daily, hyperspectral coverage of Earth’s surface, plus hyperspectral and hyperangular polarimetry. PACE is a comprehensive Earth System mission, delivering all new, space-based information on the health and diversity of aquatic and terrestrial life (algae, plants), aerosol properties & modes (e.g. smoke, dust), cloud types, and more.


The Ocean Color Instrument (OCI), PACE's primary sensor, is a hyperspectral (5 nm resolution) imaging spectrometer that measures properties of light from the ultraviolet (UV, 340 nm) through visible and near infrared (NIR, 895 nm) portions of the electromagnetic spectrum in 1.25 to 2.5 nm steps, plus 7 shortwave infrared (SWIR) bands (Werdell et al. 2019). Observations from OCI are moderate spatial resolution (1.2 km2), enabling a relatively frequent revisit time of 1-2 days. This combination of continuous, global coverage and spectral capabilities is unmatched by any other satellite platform, public or private. PACE benefits society by expanding our foundational knowledge of Earth and enabling novel, space-based science and applications tools across water resources (e.g. fisheries), air quality, land monitoring & management, and more.

PACE benefits society by expanding our foundational knowledge of Earth and enabling novel, space-based science and applications tools across water resources (e.g. fisheries), air quality, land monitoring & management, and more.


How is bbp (442) calculated and what does it represent?
Inherent optical properties (IOPs; spectral absorption and backscattering coefficients) help us understand how different wavelengths (colors) of light are scattered and absorbed by materials present in natural waters such as lakes, coastal waters, and the ocean. Unlike apparent optical properties (AOPs), IOPs are independent of the surrounding light field or viewing geometry. The different constituents in natural waters - including the water itself, phytoplankton, dissolved matter, and non-algal particulate matter - absorb and scatter light in different ways due to factors such as shape, size, and pigmentation. The types and relative concentrations of constituent matter drive the character of the light reflected from the water making IOPs key parameters in understanding marine biogeochemical processes and the characteristics of the under-water light field.


The current default configuration of the Generalized Inherent Optical Properties (GIOP-DC; Werdell et al. 2013) algorithm used to derive this data layer is based on a scientific understanding of the physics of light in water, relating IOPs to the light reflected from the ocean that is observed by space-borne sensors. The GIOP-DC input variables include spectral remote sensing reflectance values and biophysical environmental conditions, and returned variables include 7 atmospherically corrected spectral IOPs of near surface waters and their uncertanty values (see ATBD for details). Of these GIOP-DC output variables, the coefficients of both particulate bacscattering and non-algal particulate plus colored dissolved organic matter at one wavelength of 442 nm (bbp (455) and adg (442), respectively, in units of meters-1) are provided here as data layers to utilize as measures of the absorption and scattering properties of a given water body.


What other PACE data layers are available?
This data layer is 1 of 11 PACE products initially selected for the Living Atlas catalog from the mission’s comprehensive aquatic, atmospheric, and terrestrial product catalog. Click here to view all 11 PACE Living Atlas imagery services. Global, hyperspectral remote sensing reflectance observations from OCI with over 250 spectral bands, and used to derive many of PACE's aquatic products, are available to download in NetCDF format from NASA Earthdata as Level 3, mapped data with 4 km2 resolution or as Level 2 granules at unprojected, native spatial resolution (1.2 km2). To learn more about obtaining PACE data from NASA, first learn about PACE data access here, next decide which product(s) you would like to use, then go to NASA Earthdata to find your product(s) of interest in NetCDF format, which can be downloaded and then imported into ArcGIS. To learn about using Earthdata Search to narrow your data product selection, watch this tutorial. An Earthdata account is needed to download data from NASA, sign up here.



How can I stay up to date with the PACE mission?

Join the PACE Community for mission news, events, new product release announcements, and to receive our newsletters.

Would you like to see imagery services for more PACE products? Please let us know here.

item.description:
This polygon feature layer represents inland water bodies in Lebanon and surrounding areas. The dataset was derived from Sentinel-2 land cover data (2024) by extracting water-related land cover classes from Esri Living Atlas of the World.

The source land cover dataset is available through Esri Living Atlas:
https://livingatlas.arcgis.com/

The data was processed by isolating water pixels, generalizing the output to a spatial resolution of 60 meters, converting the raster into polygon features, and filtering out small polygons with an area less than 100,000 square meters. Additional attributes were introduced to store English and Arabic names for major lakes and reservoirs.

This dataset provides a generalized representation of significant inland water bodies and is suitable for cartographic display, regional analysis, and thematic mapping. Due to the classification-based source and spatial generalization, the dataset is not intended for detailed hydrological modeling, engineering applications, or legal boundary delineation.

This layer was created, processed, and published in 2026 by Esri Lebanon as part of the Lebanon Atlas initiative.

item.description: The biodiversity hotspots are regions known to hold especially high numbers of species found nowhere else, yet their remaining habitat combined covers a little more than two percent of Earth's land surface. According to the criteria developed by Myers et al. (2000), a hotspot must meet two thresholds in order to qualify: 1) it must have at least 1500 endemic, native vascular plant species, and 2) it must have already lost at least 70% of its primary, native vegetation. In the updated analysis, Mittermeier et al. (2004) recognize 34 hotspots which together hold 50% of the world's plant species and 42% of all terrestrial vertebrates as endemics. As evidence of their urgency for global conservation, hotspots also hold exceptionally high numbers of threatened vertebrates, including 50% of threatened mammals, 73% of threatened birds and 79% of threatened amphibians as endemics. There are an estimated two billion people living in the hotspots, with 300 million people within less than 10 km of existing protected areas.

The Global Power Plant Database is a comprehensive, open source database of power plants around the world. It centralizes power plant data to make it easier to navigate, compare and draw insights. Each power plant is geolocated and entries contain information on plant capacity, generation, ownership, and fuel type. As of April 2018, the database includes around 25,500 power plants from 162 countries. It will be continuously updated as data becomes available.

The methodology for the dataset creation is given in the World Resources Institute publication "A Global Database of Power Plants": http://www.wri.org/publication/global-power-plant-database

Associated code for the creation of the dataset can be found on GitHub: https://github.com/wri/global-power-plant-database

The database can be visualized on Resource Watch together with hundreds of other datasets: http://goo.gl/XMyMLt

China power plant data is currently under review and not included in the first release of the Global Power Plant Database. For the most comprehensive data about Chinese coal plants, please see the Global Coal Plant Tracker at https://endcoal.org/tracker/. For non-coal data, please sign up for our newsletter for the release announcement https://goo.gl/ivTvkd.

item.description:
About the transit accessibility map layer

What is this map layer?

This map layer presents the public transit accessibility score for an area based on walking. The score is based on a model developed by Esri that utilizes GTFS transit stop data, point business locations, and the ArcGIS StreetMap Premium street network. Individual business point locations are evaluated and scored based on multiple criteria to determine transit accessibility. The individual scores are then aggregated to an Uber H3 hexagon grid, and a mean accessibility score is assigned for each hexagon. 

Note: some hexagons do not contain any business locations, so do not have a value assigned.

What criteria determine transit accessibility?

There are many factors that may be considered for transit accessibility. To develop our model, Esri focused on the following questions:

  • Is the location close to one or more transit stops?​ How close?
  • How many unique transit routes service the location?​
  • What is the frequency of transit service at the location?​
  • Is off-hour transit service available? ​


Most of the information used to determine transit accessibility comes from General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS) stops data. In this case, Esri utilized GTFS data from Valley Metro. GTFS is a well known data standard in the transit community that captures important transit details such as stop location, transit routes servicing a stop, times of service, and wheelchair accessibility. Esri leveraged the ArcGIS Pro Composite Index tool with the GTFS data, walking distances, and business locations as inputs to arrive at the transit accessibility score.  

Why is transit accessibility important?

Understanding transit accessibility in an area allows users to:

  • Identify transit gaps​ - for instance, where workers may have a difficult time getting to their jobs
  • Optimize plans for new service or expansion​ based on where service is needed
  • Plan for special events, as detailed in this blog about planning for the LA28 Olympics
  • Identify potential economic development opportunities for businesses to locate near transit facilities such as train stations


The details: creating and interpreting the score

The accessibility score is created by generating a z-score for each point location. The z-score for each location is then aggregated within each hexagonal spatial unit to produce a mean z-score per hexagon feature. The raw z-score is also converted to a more readily understandable percentile value because these are easy to read (0-100 values) and don't rely on a normal-curve assumption, so they work even when the data are skewed. Finally, the scores are bucketed into qualitative categories such as ‘high’ and ‘low’. 

In summary, the transit accessibility is represented in three ways:

  1. Mean Z-Score – a standardized measure of accessibility.
  2. Percentile – derived from the z-score, indicating relative accessibility on a 0-100 scale.
  3. Category Classification – a qualitative label (e.g., Low, Moderate, High Accessibility).


For example, if a hexagon has a mean z-score of 1.36, this corresponds to the 90.01st percentile. This means that locations within this hexagon are more accessible by public transportation than 90% of all hexagons in the metro region. Based on this percentile, the hexagon is classified as having “High Accessibility.” 

Category scoring system for this model:

  • High Accessibility: > 70th percentile (z-score above 0.52)
  • Moderate Accessibility: 50 - 70th percentile (z-score between 0 & 0.52)
  • Fair Accessibility: 30 - 50th percentile (z-score between -0.52 & 0)
  • Low Accessibility:15 - 30th percentile (z-score between -1.04 & -0.52)
  • Not Accessible: < 15 % (z-score below -1.04)


The methodology can be applied to any transit metro region with GTFS data! To better understand why an area scores high or low, add the World Transit Stops map layer into the map to provide important context to the hexagon scores.

Publicly available GTFS datasets

  • Valley Metro - Phoenix, AZ (Public Domain - City of Phoenix Open Data)


Other Esri transit resources

  • World Transit Stops
  • World Transit Lines by Modality
  • World Transit Lines by Agency Color
  • World Transit Viewer (Web Mapping Application)

item.description:
What it shows: A Bahamas-only soil pH layer representing estimated soil pH in the upper 0–5 cm of soil. Soil pH indicates whether soil conditions are acidic, neutral, or alkaline and can influence nutrient availability and crop suitability.

How it was made: The source layer was taken from the ArcGIS Living Atlas World Soils 250m pH dataset and constrained to the 0–5 cm depth interval. For this project, the world layer was clipped to The Bahamas to create a Bahamas only screening layer for use in the FarmSmart / EDCMP web app.

Intended use: Screening-level agricultural context to support interpretation of possible acidity or alkalinity patterns when viewed together with farm locations, soil texture, NDVI baseline, and other planning layers.

Limitations: This is a generalized 250 m screening layer and not a field soil test. Local pH can vary materially within farms and between management zones. The layer should not be used as a substitute for field sampling, laboratory testing, site-specific soil amendment design, or regulatory decision-making.

Data currency: Derived from the ArcGIS Living Atlas World Soils 250m pH layer and clipped for this delivery in Jan 2026.

item.accessInformation: Bioscience, An Ecoregions-Based Approach to Protecting Half the Terrestrial Realm DOI: https://doi.org/10.1093/biosci/bix014
item.description:
Ecoregions, in the simplest definition, are ecosystems of regional extent. Specifically, ecoregions represent distinct assemblages of biodiversity―all taxa, not just vegetation―whose boundaries include the space required to sustain ecological processes. Ecoregions provide a useful basemap for conservation planning in particular because they draw on natural, rather than political, boundaries, define distinct biogeographic assemblages and ecological habitats within biomes, and assist in representation of Earth’s biodiversity.

This dataset is based on recent advances in biogeography - the science concerning the distribution of plants and animals. The original ecoregions dataset has been widely used since its introduction in 2001, underpinning the most recent analyses of the effects of global climate change on nature by ecologists to the distribution of the world's beetles to modern conservation planning.

The 846 terrestrial ecoregions are grouped into 14 biomes and 8 realms. Six of these biomes are forest biomes and remaining eight are non-forest biomes. For the forest biomes, the geographic boundaries of the ecoregions (Dinerstein et al., 2017) and protected areas (UNEP-WCMC 2016) were intersected with the Global Forest Change data (Hansen et al. 2013) for the years 2000 to 2015, to calculate percent of habitat in protected areas and percent of remaining habitat outside protected areas. Likewise, the boundaries of the non-forest ecoregions and protected areas (UNEP-WCMC 2016) were intersected with Anthropogenic Biomes data (Anthromes v2) for the year 2000 (Ellis et al., 2010) to identify remaining habitats inside and outside the protected areas. Each ecoregion has a unique ID, area (sq. degrees), and NNH (Nature Needs Half) categories 1-4. NNH categories are based on percent of habitat in protected areas and percent of remaining habitat outside protected areas.

Half Protected: More than 50% of the total ecoregion area is already protected.

Nature Could Reach Half: Less than 50% of the total ecoregion area is protected but the amount of remaining unprotected natural habitat could bring protection to over 50% if new conservation areas are added to the system.

Nature Could Recover: The amount of protected and unprotected natural habitat remaining is less than 50% but more than 20%. Ecoregions in this category would require restoration to reach Half Protected.

Nature Imperilled: The amount of protected and unprotected natural habitat remaining is less than or equal to 20%. Achieving half protected is not possible in the short term and efforts should focus on conserving remaining, native habitat fragments.

The updated Ecoregions 2017 is the most-up-to-date (as of February 2018) dataset on remaining habitat in each terrestrial ecoregion. It was released to chart progress towards achieving the visionary goal of Nature Needs Half, to protect half of all the land on Earth to save a living terrestrial biosphere.

Note - a number of ecoregions are very complex polygons with over a million vertices, such as Rock & Ice.

title:"World Ecological Land Units"

item.accessInformation: Source: USGS, Esri, Metzger et al. 2012, ESA, GEO
item.description:
Ecological Land Units (ELUs) are areas of distinct bioclimate, landform, lithology, and land cover that form the basic components of terrestrial ecosystem structure. The ELU map for 2015 was produced by combining the values in four 250m cell-sized rasters using the ArcGIS Combine tool (Spatial Analyst). These four components resulted in 3,639 different combinations or ELUs.
 
This 2015 map contains updates to the 2014 map in the form of landforms and land cover data, which have greater variety of classes and better spatial coherence (less arbitrary fragmentation).
 
These four component datasets represent the most accurate, current, globally comprehensive, and finest spatial and thematic resolution data available for each of the four inputs. Each combination was assigned a color using an algorithm that blended traditional color schemes for each of the four components. 
 
Values for each of the four input layers are listed in the table below. Every point in this map is symbolized by a combination of values for each of these fields.
 
 
Dataset Summary
This layer provides access to a cached map service created by Esri in partnership with U.S. Geological Survey's Climate and Land Use Change Program. The work from this collaboration is documented in the publication:
 
Sayre and others. 2014. A New Map of Global Ecological Land Units — An Ecophysiographic Stratification Approach. Washington, DC: Association of American Geographers. 46 pages. 
 
What can you do with this layer?
This map is intended to work as an ecological background map in conjunction with the reference layers of various ArcGIS Online base maps, and supports visualization tasks in ArcGIS Online and Desktop. 
 
An image service is available on ArcGIS Online that provides access to a 250m cell-sized raster of the World Ecophysiographic Land Units. The image service provides access to the data underlying this map. The image service can be used as an input to geoprocessing and to support pop-ups that can be used with this map online.
 
A service is available to the data tables associated with this map as well as other global layers. These data table services can be used by developers to create custom applications. For more information see the World Ecophysiographic Tables.
 
The Living Atlas of the World provides an easy way to explore the landscape layers and many other beautiful and authoritative maps on hundreds of topics.

item.accessInformation: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Ocean Ecology Laboratory, Ocean Biology Processing Group. PACE Ocean Color Instrument Level-3 Mapped Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), Version 3.1 Data; NASA OB.DAAC, Greenbelt, MD, USA.
item.description:
Overview

Terrestrial Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) from the NASA Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) Ocean Color Instrument (OCI). NDVI is calculated as (Rnir-Rred)/(Rnir+Rred), where Rnir is a near infrared spectral band and Rred is a red spectral band. PACE NDVI is processed to be similar to MODerate resolution Imaging Spectraradiometer (MODIS) NDVI data by using an average of OCI bands between 841 and 877 nanometers (nm) for the Rnir band and between 620 and 671 nm for the Rred band. See Mathematical Theory section of the Caplan et al. 2025 algorithm documentation for equation details. Data provided as global, 8-day averages mapped to a standard, equal-angle, latitude-longitude grid of 0.02 degrees, which equates to approximately 2 kilometers (km) at the equator. Data has been corrected for atmospheric scattering and absorption. Pixels with no data values are masked (excluded) due to presence of water, cloud cover, or other features marked by quality control flags as described below.

Intended Use: What can I do with this layer?
NDVI has been used for decades describe seasonal and annual changes over time (Huang et al., 2021). In this way you can utilize NDVI to monitor vegetation amounts, changes in vegetation cover (e.g. post-fire recovery, deforestation), as a proxy of health, among others. The time (8 day average) and space (2km2) resolution of this data layer enables weekly to seasonal and annual insight at local to global scales.
 

Limitations of Use: What should I know about the data?
Data Status (Maturity): This product is provisional, which means that product results have been reviewed and are in family with heritage data products or other basis of expectation, but have not yet been extensively validated and so may still contain significant errors. Data layer is sufficient for qualitative determinations of product fitness-for-purpose, for testing by operational users, and may be suitable for scientific publication.

Data Masking: This is a Level 3, globally-binned product from NASA’s Ocean Biology Processing Group (OBPG). By default, OBPG Level 3 data values are masked (value is set to null, or no data) according to a standard set of quality control parameters. Please see Level 3 Algorithm Usage Constraints from the Caplan et al. 2025 algorithm documentation for masking parameter details.
 

Where do I go with further questions?
Visit NASA’s Earthdata Forum where users can post questions that are answered by the personnel working at NASA with the PACE mission and/or the Ocean Biology Distributed Active Archive Center (OB.DAAC) that processes and distributes PACE data. First, follow this link to view only “PACE” and “OBDAAC” tagged questions on the Earthdata Forum. Then search and read through previous posts for your question. If it has not yet been asked please post your question in the Forum and be sure "PACE" and "OBDAAC" filter tags are applied.
 

 

Mission and Product Background

PACE Mission Overview:
Launched in February 2024, NASA’s Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) observatory uniquely provides near-daily, hyperspectral coverage of Earth’s surface, plus hyperspectral and hyperangular polarimetry. PACE is a comprehensive Earth System mission, delivering all new, space-based information on the health and diversity of aquatic and terrestrial life (algae, plants), aerosol properties & modes (e.g. smoke, dust), cloud types, and more.

The Ocean Color Instrument (OCI), PACE's primary sensor, is a hyperspectral (5 nm resolution) imaging spectrometer that measures properties of light from the ultraviolet (UV, 340 nm) through visible and near infrared (NIR, 895 nm) portions of the electromagnetic spectrum in 1.25 to 2.5 nm steps, plus 7 shortwave infrared (SWIR) bands (Werdell et al. 2019). Observations from OCI are moderate spatial resolution (1.2 km2), enabling a relatively frequent revisit time of 1-2 days. This combination of continuous, global coverage and spectral capabilities is unmatched by any other satellite platform, public or private. PACE benefits society by expanding our foundational knowledge of Earth and enabling novel, space-based science and applications tools across water resources (e.g. fisheries), air quality, land monitoring & management, and more.

 

Terrestrial Remote Sensing from an Ocean Color Sensor?
Designed and optimized to operate across a broad dynamic range, from the dark target of the ocean to bright, highly reflective cloud tops, PACE’s OCI also collects surface reflectance data from the world's terrestrial environments across 122 bands, resolving spectral properties of the Earth more finely than previous multispectral missions could achieve. Work thus far has demonstrated viability of OCI’s land data products for terrestrial investigations (e.g. Caplan and Huemmrich 2025; Huemmrich et al. 2025).

OCI’s coverage and capabilities enable provision of both novel, hyperspectral-enabled land observations as well as maintenance and extension of certain historical multispectral data records. Advanced vegetation indexes (VIs) enabled by OCI’s narrow-wavelength surface reflectance measurements provide continuous, synoptic insights into foliar pigment amounts (chlorophylls, carotenoids, and anthocyanins), water content, and photosynthetic light use efficiency across the globe each day. Heritage VIs (e.g., normalized difference vegetation index, NDVI; reviewed in Huang et al. 2021) can also be calculated by aggregating (averaging) OCI’s narrow bandwidths across ranges that approximate the multi-spectral, broadband reflectances of instruments such as MODIS, see the Mathematical Theory section of the Caplan et al. 2025 algorithm documentation for details. See the full list of heritage and hyperspectral-enabled VIs produced by PACE here.

 

What other PACE data layers are available?
This data layer is 1 of 11 PACE products initially selected for the Living Atlas catalog from the mission’s comprehensive aquatic, atmospheric, and terrestrial product catalog. Click here to view all 11 PACE Living Atlas imagery services. The Level 3, 122-band hyperspectral surface reflectance data (SFREFL) used to derive all VIs is available from NASA Earthdata to download at 2 kilometer resolution in NetCDF format. To learn more about obtaining PACE data from NASA, first learn about PACE data access here, next decide which product(s) you would like to use, then go to NASA Earthdata to find your product(s) of interest in NetCDF format, which can be downloaded and then imported into ArcGIS. To learn about using Earthdata Search to narrow your data product selection, watch this tutorial. An Earthdata account is needed to download data from NASA, sign up here.

item.description:
In geography, an antipode is the exact other side of the world from any given location. When I was a kid, we always used to talk about digging a hole so deep that you'd exit in China. But we foolish Michigan kids didn't realize that if we really dug a hole straight down, presuming we survived the magnificent heat of Earth's core, eventually we'd pop out at the bottom of the southern Indian Ocean and drown.
Antipodes can be a fun and engaging teaching mechanism for geography students. It helps us...wrap...our minds around our roundish planet, and it burns some spatial thinking calories.

This layer is sourced from Natural Earth, and was converted into an antipode version of itself via this process.
Here is an Antipode World Countries polygon layer.

item.description:
Mature Support Notice: This item is in mature support as of April 2026. A replacement item has not been identified at this time. Esri recommends updating your maps and apps to phase out use of this item.
 
Measurements of surface air and ocean temperature are compiled from around the world each month by NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information and are analyzed and compared to the 1971-2000 average temperature for each location. The resulting temperature anomaly (or difference from the average) is shown in this feature service. The 2025 values are the last that will be included and no future updates are planned.    
 
The NOAAGlobalTemp dataset  is the official U.S. long-term record of global temperature data and is often used to show trends in temperature change around the world. It combines thousands of land-based station measurements from the Global Historical Climatology Network (GHCN) along with surface ocean temperature from the Extended Reconstructed Sea Surface Temperature (ERSST) analysis. These two datasets are merged into a 5-degree resolution product. A report that summarizes the data is released each month (and end of the year) by NOAA NCEI is available here.  
 
GHCN monthly mean averages for temperature and precipitation for the 1981-2010 period are also available in Living Atlas here. 
 
 
What can you do with this layer? 
 
Visualization: This layer can be used to plot areas where temperature was higher or lower than the historical average for the past month.  
 
Analysis: The full archive from 1880 – present is available here, and can be used as an input to a variety of geoprocessing tools, such as Space Time Cubes and other trend analyses.

Original data sources include the Instituto Geográfico Nacional, Ministerio de Agricultura, Alimentación y Medio Ambiente, and Esri.
item.description:
This dataset represents a land cover and environmental characterization of Castellón Province (Spain) using a hexagonal grid of 5 square kilometers per cell, derived from a national-scale dataset published in the ArcGIS Living Atlas.

The original dataset characterizes the Spanish territory by associating each hexagon with multiple environmental indicators obtained through spatial analysis, including:

  • Mean elevation and slope derived from the 5-meter Digital Terrain Model (Instituto Geográfico Nacional)
  • Natura 2000 protected areas (Ministerio de Agricultura, Alimentación y Medio Ambiente)
  • Hydrological influence areas derived from main river networks
  • Corine Land Cover 2012 land cover typologies

For this product, the dataset was spatially clipped to the administrative extent of Castellón Province and published as a feature layer in ArcGIS Hub.
No changes were made to the original attributes or data structure beyond spatial subsetting.

This dataset is intended for territorial analysis, visualization, and educational purposes.

item.description:
Region-level analysis to cluster areas of biodiversity significance; generated based on five ecological criteria i.e.,(1) fragile and sensitive habitat (the coverage of biogenic habitats: coral reefs, seagrass and mangrove); (2) species richness (modeled geographic distributions of 10,672 species ranges and occurrence records of 19,251 species); (3) the presence of species of conservation concern (distributions of 834 species of special conservation concern; (4) the occurrence of restricted-range species (distributions of 373 restricted-range reef fish species); and (6) areas of importance for particular life history stages (distribution of six species of sea turtle).

 

The datasets were clipped to the CT region using a grid approach of half-degree cells (0.5°), where each cell covered an area of ~ 55 x 55 km. All of the datasets obtained from each criterion were superimposed to produce an integrated dataset. The cluster of biodiversity hotspot areas were analyzed based on the biodiversity score of each cell.  The score of each criterion was calculated based on the total number of habitat, species or species index that fell within each cell.

 

We analyzed the cluster of areas of biodiversity importance using the hotspots analysis tools ESRI in ArcGIS. The hotspots tools is a spatial statistical mapping tool that identifies the spatial patterns of data based on the Getis-Ord GI* statistics (ESRI, 2016b; Getis & Ord, 1992; Ord & Getis, 1995). The hotspots analysis identifies whether cells with high scores or cells with low scores tend to be clustered in the study area. The statistically significant Z score (GI* statistics) were analyzed by comparing the local sum of a cell’s score and its neighbors proportionally to the sum of all cells’ scores. For statistically significant positive Z scores, the larger the Z score, the more intense the clustering of high scores (hotspots).  For statistically significant negative Z scores, the smaller the Z score, the more intense the clustering of low scores (coldspots). The hotspots analysis clustered the area into three classes of hotspots (99%, 95% and, 90% confidence level), three classes of coldspots (99%, 95% and 90% confidence level) and one class of not statistically significant clusters.

item.accessInformation: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Ocean Ecology Laboratory, Ocean Biology Processing Group. PACE Ocean Color Instrument Level-3 Mapped Photochemical Reflectance Index (PRI), Version 3.1 Data; NASA OB.DAAC, Greenbelt, MD, USA.
item.description:
Overview

Terrestrial Photochemical Reflectance Index (PRI) from the NASA Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) Ocean Color Instrument (OCI). PRI is a normalized difference ratio of two narrow visible wavelengths expressed as: (R531 – R570)/(R531 + R570), where R531 is the reflectance at 531 nanometers (nm), the band sensitive to the epoxidation state of the xanthophyll cycle pigments, and R570 is a reference band at 570 nm (Grace et al. 2007, Coops et al. 2010). Data provided as global, 8-day averages mapped to a standard, equal-angle, latitude-longitude grid of 0.02 degrees, which equates to ~2 kilometers (km) at the equator. Data has been corrected for atmospheric scattering and absorption. Pixels with no data values are masked (excluded) due to presence of water, cloud cover, or other features marked by quality control flags as described below.

Intended Use: What can I do with this layer?
PRI has been related to foliage or ecosystem photosynthetic light use efficiency (LUE). Its response is driven by leaf-level reflectance changes associated with changes in pigment pools in response to stresses although it can also be affected by changes in leaf area (Grace et al. 2007, Coops et al. 2010). The time (8 day average) and space (2 km2) resolution of this data layer enables weekly to seasonal and annual insight at local to global scales.
 

Limitations of Use: What should I know about the data?
Data Status (Maturity): This product is provisional, which means that product results have been reviewed and are in family with heritage data products or other basis of expectation, but have not yet been extensively validated and so may still contain significant errors. Data layer is sufficient for qualitative determinations of product fitness-for-purpose, for testing by operational users, and may be suitable for scientific publication.

Data Masking: This is a Level 3, globally-binned product from NASA’s Ocean Biology Processing Group (OBPG). By default, OBPG Level 3 data values are masked (value is set to null, or no data) according to a standard set of quality control parameters. Please see Level 3 Algorithm Usage Constraints for masking parameter details.

Algorithm Theoretical Basis Document (ATBD): See ATBD for algorithm details including scientific theory, calculations, etc. https://doi.org/10.5067/8L77O0Y8GHV8.

 

Where do I go with further questions?
Visit NASA’s Earthdata Forum where users can post questions that are answered by the personnel working at NASA with the PACE mission and/or the Ocean Biology Distributed Active Archive Center (OB.DAAC) that processes and distributes PACE data. First, follow this link to view only “PACE” and “OBDAAC” tagged questions on the Earthdata Forum. Then search and read through previous posts for your question. If it has not yet been asked please post your question in the Forum and be sure "PACE" and "OBDAAC" filter tags are applied.
 

 

Mission and Product Background

PACE Mission Overview:
Launched in February 2024, NASA’s Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) observatory uniquely provides near-daily, hyperspectral coverage of Earth’s surface, plus hyperspectral and hyperangular polarimetry. PACE is a comprehensive Earth System mission, delivering all new, space-based information on the health and diversity of aquatic and terrestrial life (algae, plants), aerosol properties & modes (e.g. smoke, dust), cloud types, and more.

The Ocean Color Instrument (OCI), PACE's primary sensor, is a hyperspectral (5 nm resolution) imaging spectrometer that measures properties of light from the ultraviolet (UV, 340 nm) through visible and near infrared (NIR, 895 nm) portions of the electromagnetic spectrum in 1.25 to 2.5 nm steps, plus 7 shortwave infrared (SWIR) bands (Werdell et al. 2019). Observations from OCI are moderate spatial resolution (1.2 km2), enabling a relatively frequent revisit time of 1-2 days. This combination of continuous, global coverage and spectral capabilities is unmatched by any other satellite platform, public or private. PACE benefits society by expanding our foundational knowledge of Earth and enabling novel, space-based science and applications tools across water resources (e.g. fisheries), air quality, land monitoring & management, and more.

 

Terrestrial Remote Sensing from an Ocean Color Sensor?
Designed and optimized to operate across a broad dynamic range, from the dark target of the ocean to bright, highly reflective cloud tops, PACE’s OCI also collects surface reflectance data from the world's terrestrial environments across 122 bands, resolving spectral properties of the Earth more finely than previous multispectral missions could achieve. Work thus far has demonstrated viability of OCI’s land data products for terrestrial investigations (Caplan et al. 2025).

OCI’s coverage and capabilities enable provision of both novel, hyperspectral-enabled land observations as well as maintenance and extension of certain historical multispectral data records. Advanced vegetation indexes (VIs) enabled by OCI’s narrow-wavelength surface reflectance measurements provide continuous, synoptic insights into foliar pigment amounts (chlorophylls, carotenoids, and anthocyanins), water content, and photosynthetic light use efficiency across the globe each day. Heritage VIs (e.g., normalized difference vegetation index, NDVI; reviewed in Huang et al. 2021) can also be calculated by aggregating (averaging) OCI’s narrow bandwidths across ranges that approximate the multi-spectral, broadband reflectances of instruments such as MODIS, see the Mathematical Theory section of the ATBD for details. See the full list of heritage and hyperspectral-enabled VIs produced by PACE here.

 

What other PACE data layers are available?
This data layer is 1 of 11 PACE products initially selected for the Living Atlas catalog from the mission’s comprehensive aquatic, atmospheric, and terrestrial product catalog. Click here to view all 11 PACE Living Atlas imagery services. The Level 3, 122-band hyperspectral surface reflectance data (SFREFL) used to derive all VIs is available from NASA Earthdata to download at 2 kilometer resolution in NetCDF format. To access PACE mission data products available from NASA, first learn about PACE data access here, next decide which PACE product(s) you would like to use, then go to NASA Earthdata to find PACE products in NetCDF format, which can be downloaded and then imported into ArcGIS. An Earthdata account is needed to download data from NASA, sign up here. To learn about using Earthdata Search to find data, watch this tutorial.

item.description:
Countries – matched boundary lines and polygons with names attributes for countries and sovereign states. Includes dependencies (French Polynesia), map units (U.S. Pacific Island Territories) and sub-national map subunits (Corsica versus mainland Metropolitan France).

Natural Earth is a convenient resource for making custom maps. Unlike other map data intended for analysis or government mapping, it is designed to meet the needs of cartographers and map designers. Maximum flexibility is a goal.

Natural Earth is a public domain collection of map datasets available at 1:10 million (large scale/more detailed), 1:50 million (medium scale/moderate detail), and 1:110 million (small scale/coarse detail) scales. It features tightly integrated vector and raster data to create a variety of visually pleasing, well-crafted maps with cartography or GIS software. Natural Earth was made possible by many volunteers and supported by NACIS.
  • Convenience – Natural Earth solves a problem: finding suitable data for making small-scale maps. In a time when the web is awash in geospatial data, cartographers are forced to waste time sifting through confusing tangles of poorly attributed data to make clean, legible maps. Because your time is valuable, Natural Earth data comes ready to use.
  • Neatness Counts – The carefully generalized linework maintains consistent, recognizable geographic shapes at 1:10m, 1:50m, and 1:110m scales. Natural Earth was built from the ground up, so you will find that all data layers align precisely with one another. For example, where rivers and country borders are one and the same, the lines are coincident.
  • GIS Attributes – Natural Earth, however, is more than just a collection of pretty lines. The data attributes are equally important for mapmaking. Most data contain embedded feature names, which are ranked by relative importance. Other attributes facilitate faster map production, such as width attributes assigned to river segments for creating tapers.
Intelligent data
The attributes assigned to Natural Earth vectors make for efficient mapmaking. Most lines and areas contain embedded feature names, which are ranked by relative importance. Up to eight rankings per data theme allow easy custom map “mashups” to emphasize your subject while de-emphasizing reference features. Other attributes focus on map design. For example, width attributes assigned to rivers allow you to create tapered drainages. Assigning different colors to contiguous country polygons is another task made easier thanks to data attribution.

Other key features
  • Vector features include name attributes and bounding box extents. Know that the Rocky Mountains are larger than the Ozarks.
  • Large polygons are split for more efficient data handling–such as bathymetric layers.
  • Projection-friendly vectors precisely match at 180 degrees longitude. Lines contain enough data points for smooth bending in conic projections, but not so many that computer processing speed suffers.
  • Raster data includes grayscale-shaded relief and cross-blended hypsometric tints derived from the latest NASA SRTM Plus elevation data and tailored to register with Natural Earth Vector.
  • Optimized for use in web mapping applications, with built-in scale attributes to assist features to be shown at different zoom levels.
How to add this layer to a map
In ArcGIS, you can easily add this layer to a map and modify it as desired.
  1. From the ArcGIS Online item page, click the button to Open in Map Viewer.
  2. From an existing ArcGIS map, browse for the layer by name or its item ID (get the ID from the item URL) and add to map.
  3. Alternatively, copy the web service URL to use it with software that supports ArcGIS REST services.
Discover more Natural Earth ready-to-use data layers on our Hub site.

item.description:
This layer contains over 28,000 power plant locations in 164 countries around the globe. Click on each power plant to view its:

  • Name
  • Fuel type: hydro, solar, wind, gas, coal, oil, biomass, waste, nuclear, cogeneration, geothermal, petcoke, storage, wave and tidal, or other
  • Capacity (MW)
  • Annual generation (GWh)
  • Data source
  • Link to more information
To view additional information such as the data source year, geolocation source, latitude, and longitude, click on the table icon underneath the layer name. 

This feature layer employs Clustering which groups point features within a certain distance of one another into one symbol. When you zoom in, the clusters start to break up and greater point details are displayed. To view the popup for individual power plants, click on the cluster and select Browse Features. 
The Firefly symbology used for this layer works best with darker basemaps like the Firefly basemap, Nova basemap, or the Human Geography Dark basemap, all found in the Living Atlas of the World. 
This layer was created by the World Resources Institute and was last updated June 2018. The dataset is updated by the World Resources Institute every 4 to 6 months. For more information, please contact Aaron Kressig at aaron.kressig@wri.org.

item.description:
This is an assessment of pedestrian accessibility in the world's main urban centers, aggregated at country level. Indicators include the average walking time to different categories of destinations, as well as the proportion of inhabitants that can access each category of services within a 15 minutes walk. The data is produced and maintained by the UN's Sustainable Development Solutions Network (SDSN) as part of the SDG Transformation Center.

Pedestrian accessibility is the extent to which the built environment supports walking access to destinations of interest. This measure is particularly useful for assessing spatial justice in cities, usually represented by underpriviledged communities which are pushed to live in deteriorated urban areas receiving a minor share of public investments and thus low levels of accessibility. Monitoring spatial indicators of pedestrian accessibility helps planners and policymakers evaluate the impacts of urban design and transport interventions and guides targeted interventions towards creating healthy, sustainable cities, and achieving the United Nations (UN) Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

Data Sources
Two main sources of data are behind this study.  OpenStreetMap  is used to collect data on pedestrian infrastructure and geographically allocated places of interest (POI): hospitals, schools, supermarkets, restaurants, schools, etc. Pedestrian infrastructure networks are returned by the OpenStreetMap API as networks of nodes and edges, where each node represents a street intersection and each edge represents a segment of road with walkable features. Data on population density for every city is retrieved from the European Commission's 2020  Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL) . This data is retrieved in the form of a grid of 100m by 100m squares and their associated population density values covering the entire world.

Geographical extent
The geographical extent of a particular city or region often varies according to different authorities and interpretations. Novel projects, such as the Global Human Settlements (GHS) Urban Centres Database (UCDB), seek to establish a consistent, shared geographic definition of “urban centres” globally. This study does not consider municipal boundaries for defining city borders. Rather, it considers "Functional Urban Areas"  as defined by the OECD and the European Commission . The boundaries of Functional Urban Areas consider urbanization factors such as commuting flows and population density, and are less arbitrary than municipal boundaries. For this reason, cities presented here may have a different (and often bigger) shape expected.

Accessibility analysis
To measure accessibility to services for each city, we perform a network analysis on the pedestrian street networks and POIs data to quantify and map accessibility to urban infrastructure at the street intersection level. For each 100m cell from the population grid data, the resulting "walking time" reflects the time that a person residing inside that cell would have to walk for, using the existing pedestrian infrastructure, to reach the first amenity from a given category of services. The analysis was performed using geopandas and pandana python packages.

These calculations were performed for all cities where at least one POI could be identified for each square kilometer. This threshold is applied in order to enforce representativity and accuracy. These scores were then be generalized for each urban center, by taking the population weighted average of the accessibility score for each point in the population grid.

Code for generating these results is publicly available at: https://github.com/sdsna/sdg-accessibility

This methodology was expanded from Nicoletti, L., Verma, T., Sirenko, M. (2022). Disadvantaged Communities Have Lower Access to Urban Infrastructure. Environment and Planning B: Urban Analytics and City Science, 0(0) and the CityAccessMap project.

item.accessInformation: "Biodiversity Hotspots 2016.1", Conservation International
item.description: The biodiversity hotspots are regions known to hold especially high numbers of species found nowhere else, yet their remaining habitat combined covers a little more than two percent of Earth's land surface. According to the criteria developed by Myers et al. (2000), a hotspot must meet two thresholds in order to qualify: 1) it must have at least 1500 endemic, native vascular plant species, and 2) it must have already lost at least 70% of its primary, native vegetation. Around the world, 36 areas qualify as hotspots. They represent just 2.4% of Earth’s land surface, but they support more than half of the world’s plant species as endemics — i.e., species found no place else — and nearly 43% of bird, mammal, reptile and amphibian species as endemics. More information at https://www.conservation.org/learning/biodiversity-hotspots

Samenvatting
The GHS-FUA R2019A dataset contains extensive information on Functional Urban Areas (FUAs) worldwide. An FUA includes both urban cores (centers) and surrounding suburban areas that are closely connected to the core city based on factors like population density, area, and surrounding regions. The data consists of polygons, which include demographic data, area delineations, and associated time periods.

The goal of the GHS-FUA R2019A dataset is to provide a consistent and globally comparable framework for analyzing urban areas. The data is updated every five years.

The GHS-FUA R2019A dataset is managed and published by the Joint Research Centre (JRC) of the European Commission. The Province of South Holland offers this data through its collaboration with METREX, a network of European metropolitan regions and areas, of which South Holland is a member.

The dataset can be applied to topics related to urban planning, policy development, and research on urban development.

item.description:
Ecological Land Units (ELUs) are areas of distinct bioclimate, landform, lithology, and land cover that form the basic components of terrestrial ecosystem structure. The ELU map was produced by by combining the values in four 250m cell-sized rasters using the ArcGIS Combine tool (Spatial Analyst). These four components resulted in 3,923 different combinations or ELUs.

These four component datasets represent the most accurate, current, globally comprehensive, and finest spatial and thematic resolution data available for each of the four inputs. Each combination was assigned a color using an algorithm that blended traditional color schemes for each of the four components. 

The layer provides access to a cached map service created by Esri in partnership with U.S. Geological Survey's Climate and Land Use Change Program. The work from this collaboration is documented in the publication:

Sayre and others. 2014. A New Map of Global Ecological Land Units — An Ecophysiographic Stratification Approach. Washington, DC: Association of American Geographers. 46 pages. Available online

item.description:
In geography, an antipode is the exact other side of the world from any given location. When I was a kid, we always used to talk about digging a hole so deep that you'd exit in China. But we foolish Michigan kids didn't realize that if we really dug a hole straight down, presuming we survived the magnificent heat of Earth's core, eventually we'd pop out at the bottom of the southern Indian Ocean and drown.
Antipodes can be a fun and engaging teaching mechanism for geography students. It helps us...wrap...our minds around our roundish planet, and it burns some spatial thinking calories.

This layer is sourced from Natural Earth, and was converted into an antipode version of itself via this process.

item.description:
Group Layer Derrived from: Ecological Land Units (ELUs) are areas of distinct bioclimate, landform, lithology, and land cover that form the basic components of terrestrial ecosystem structure. The ELU map for 2015 was produced by combining the values in four 250m cell-sized rasters using the ArcGIS Combine tool (Spatial Analyst). These four components resulted in 3,639 different combinations or ELUs.
 
This 2015 map contains updates to the 2014 map in the form of landforms and land cover data, which have greater variety of classes and better spatial coherence (less arbitrary fragmentation).
 
 
These four component datasets represent the most accurate, current, globally comprehensive, and finest spatial and thematic resolution data available for each of the four inputs. Each combination was assigned a color using an algorithm that blended traditional color schemes for each of the four components. 
 
Values for each of the four input layers are listed in the table below. Every point in this map is symbolized by a combination of values for each of these fields.
 
 
Dataset Summary
 
This layer provides access to a cached map service created by Esri in partnership with U.S. Geological Survey's Climate and Land Use Change Program. The work from this collaboration is documented in the publication:
 
Sayre and others. 2014. A New Map of Global Ecological Land Units — An Ecophysiographic Stratification Approach. Washington, DC: Association of American Geographers. 46 pages. 
 
 
What can you do with this layer?
 
This map is intended to work as an ecological background map in conjunction with the reference layers of various ArcGIS Online base maps, and supports visualization tasks in ArcGIS Online and Desktop. 
 
This layer is part of a larger collection of landscape layers that you can use to perform a wide variety of mapping and analysis tasks.
 
 
An image service is available on ArcGIS Online that provides access to a 250m cell-sized raster of the World Ecophysiographic Land Units. The image service provides access to the data underlying this map. The image service can be used as an input to geoprocessing and to support pop-ups that can be used with this map online.
 
A service is available to the data tables associated with this map as well as other global layers. These data table services can be used by developers to create custom applications. For more information see the World Ecophysiographic Tables.
 
Layers providing access to the four input layers used to create this map see the following links:

item.snippet: The biodiversity hotspots are regions known to hold especially high numbers of species found nowhere else, yet their remaining habitat combined covers a little more than two percent of Earth's land surface. According to the criteria developed by Myers et al. (2000), a hotspot must meet two thresholds in order to qualify: 1) it must have at least 1500 endemic, native vascular plant species, and 2) it must have already lost at least 70% of its primary, native vegetation. In the updated analysis, Mittermeier et al. (2004) recognize 34 hotspots which together hold 50% of the world's plant species and 42% of all terrestrial vertebrates as endemics. As evidence of their urgency for global conservation, hotspots also hold exceptionally high numbers of threatened vertebrates, including 50% of threatened mammals, 73% of threatened birds and 79% of threatened amphibians as endemics. There are an estimated two billion people living in the hotspots, with 300 million people within less than 10 km of existing protected areas.
